item.title: Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
item.description: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident , tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog. The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata. The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported e arlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel. Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release. Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest. And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

item.title: Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed
item.description: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register , the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. In a separate public statement , Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed. Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications. "The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email. While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions. Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register : "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

item.title: The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't
item.description: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value. A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity. Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models. If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist. Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course. Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says. item.title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways
item.description: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required . Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's requirments, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. item.title: Who can still open your files after they've left?
item.description: Someone left your organisation in the spring. Can they still open the project share? Most infrastructure leads would want to check before answering, and that pause is the subject of a dinner The Register and LucidLink are hosting for senior technology, infrastructure, and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. Request a place The trouble is the copies. A busy folder lives on the file server, in a sync client, on a couple of laptops and in the share set up for an agency last year, and each copy carries its own permissions. Locking down one leaves the others as they were. Then there's the tool a team built for itself because the approved one was too slow, which IT may not know exists. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, and that's what makes it worth going. People say what actually happened in their own shop and how they caught it. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers round the table. Nobody presents. The talk moves on to unstructured data that keeps growing, the duplicate storage that comes with it, and how to get access back under control without throwing out the storage and governance you've already paid for. Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited. Request a place at the 24 November dinner Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally. item.title: Japanese homeware giant pulls online store after cloud breach puts 7.7M records at risk
item.description: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders. The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29 , a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation. Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access. Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns. The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers. Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity. There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised. It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ , Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion. Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed. Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected. Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer. The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

item.title: AI echo chambers and sanity in tech leadership: Three case studies
item.description: "AI delusion" remains loosely defined, but most of us know it when we see it: exaggerated faith in the technology's power, applicability, or nature, coupled with a refusal to acknowledge its limitations. It's bad in the individual, as when an elderly relative emails you a hallucination-laden ChatGPT summary. It's worse in management, when your boss insists that AI slop is genius marketing content at a bargain rate. It is terrifying in tech CEOs. It is not, thankfully, compulsory. Consider three recent examples of technology leadership in the age of AI. One would be Pythonesque were the disconnect with engineers and the public not so profound. Another risks becoming a business-school case study in how to demolish customer trust. The third offers something less fashionable: robust pragmatism. Saving the best till last, y'all. Case 1: we present for your consideration Sam Altman of OpenAI, one of the few actually at the controls of the singularity machine. It seems churlish to pluck just one luscious fruit out of that cornucopia of choices, yet we must. Sam Altman thinks it is a sin against the natural order that so much RAM is idling in machines owned by individuals, organizations, and anywhere that isn't Big AI . It's oh so inefficient. How convenient that the efficient allocation of scarce resources should favor the business he runs. Free market schmarket. Altman has since said his remarks were taken out of context and that he wants consumers to have as much memory as they like. The efficiency argument still reveals whose priorities come first. This is the best kind of delusion, one with an undeniable truth at its core – memory does indeed get used far more intensively in AI model makers and inference servers than in your laptop. For a business selling the future, treating privately owned hardware as an inefficient allocation of resources has a distinctly Soviet flavor, and the American right has vowed to stamp out socialist extremism. Get on with it, chaps, you've only got two years left . That Altman can't see this is the best bit of the misconception. There are two potential root causes of this Marxist-Leninist-Altmanism. One is that he's mathed the math and worked out that the only way OpenAI can hit the numbers is if it gets every last byte in the world, hot off the fab. The other is that you can't run on-prem on an 8 GB state-mandated Chromebook, and on-prem is otherwise going to twist his melon until it falls off. item.title: Portal breach at Germany's top university exposes every registered user's password
item.description: Attackers stole central university login passwords belonging to everyone registered with the Technical University of Munich's myTUM portal, including an admin whose credentials were then used to attack a second system. TUM restored access to its TUMonline campus management system on Monday morning, allowing users to change their passwords. The university disclosed the attack on November 6. The initial attack targeted the myTUM portal, which serves students and faculty members, providing centralized online access to services and documents. TUM said the attackers used the admin's credentials to launch a follow-on attack on TUMonline, its central campus management system, which forced the IT team to take it offline. The university has not disclosed how the attackers initially gained access or how the stolen passwords were stored. It did not immediately answer questions about the number of affected users. It also did not specify whether this sysadmin had multi-factor authentication (MFA) switched on, but it confirmed that "user accounts with MFA were protected from this attack." Attackers may also have accessed names, home addresses, and dates of birth. Potentially exposed employee records included work addresses and phone numbers, while student records included ID numbers, degree programs, and completed semesters. "The attackers' access within TUMonline was largely logged," said Dr Alexander Braun, CIO at TUM, in the disclosure. "After analyzing these logs, we currently assume that no other data from TUMonline was compromised, such as grades or college applications. We are continuing to investigate this." TUM is directing users to reset their passwords through Microsoft 365 where possible. Those without MFA already configured must instead use a German electronic ID or request a reset email while connected to the campus network. The university also warned users to watch for phishing and fraud, and to change any passwords reused elsewhere. TUM ranks first in Germany and 25th worldwide in the QS university rankings. The STEM-focused institution reports 51,954 students across its German campuses and TUM Asia in Singapore, plus 12,850 employees. ®

item.title: AI Slop FM radio experiment puts machines on trial, one dodgy tune at a time
item.description: A Welsh music enthusiast has built an internet radio station that plays AI-generated tunes alongside human-made tracks without telling listeners which is which, to find out whether listeners really hate AI music or just the idea of it. AI Slop FM is the creation of Mike Chaffin, who built and runs the station single-handedly from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire. By stripping away artist names, cover art, and any mention of AI, Chaffin hopes to find out what listeners really think when they have nothing but the music to go on. The free 24/7 station asks listeners to rate tracks from S to E, tag how the music makes them feel, and leave written feedback. The most popular submissions will eventually make it into a weekly chart called the Slop 40, giving creators something that can be hard to come by in the age of streaming: an actual audience. Anyone can submit a track, including human musicians, although Chaffin has already discovered that not all of them are particularly keen on the idea. He told The Register that he had floated the idea to an unsigned musician friend who had sold around 600 albums, but was met with a rather nervous response. "Wh, wh, why would I want to do that?" the musician reportedly asked, according to Chaffin, who said he had never heard his friend stutter before. "It seems that there is a deep rooted fear of AI music in the industry," Chaffin said. The station is still in beta, with Chaffin waiting for enough submissions to fill its schedule across different genres before opening it fully. He's already been pleasantly surprised by the quality of the music submitted, although he still listens to every track to make sure nobody is trying to pass off Bohemian Rhapsody as their own work. Among the early offerings are what Chaffin describes as a developing genre of slightly rude protest songs about HR departments, along with an operatic epic about a blocked toilet. "Some of which are hilarious," he said of the HR songs. As for the toilet opera, it "runs through my head about once a day, whether I like it or not." Chaffin believes the sheer volume of music uploaded to streaming platforms means plenty of perfectly decent tracks never find an audience, whether a person or a machine made them. He hopes AI Slop FM will give some of those overlooked creations a chance to be heard. "You don't have to have published your creations to upload. Just to own the rights," he explained. Tracks that don't make the Slop 40 could still get another outing, with plans for genre-specific stations offering unsuccessful submissions a second chance. The bigger question is what happens when listeners start rating AI-generated music more highly than the human competition, but Chaffin isn't particularly worried about that. item.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
item.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

item.title: Memory crunch makes refurbished kit look a lot less secondhand
item.description: Rising memory prices are pushing more customers toward refurbished tech, suppliers say, with warranties of up to three years helping to make secondhand kit a less daunting purchase. Memory costs have more than quadrupled this year as manufacturers prioritize more lucrative high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for servers powering AI datacenters. Many enterprises are keeping equipment longer in an uncertain economy. Ben Caddy, senior analyst at Omdia, said suppliers were linking refresh discussions with opportunities to recover value from customers' aging kit. By 2030, he predicted, 35 percent of "all the hardware sold for the channel will be taken back by partners," driven "by the sheer economic logic of taking equipment back, recovering value, and embracing more circular IT lifecycles." This is already helping some customers "unlock some capital to put towards those [relatively] small refresh plans," he said while hosting a panel on circular IT at last month's Canalys Forums in Barcelona. Refurbished smartphones are growing in popularity, but persuading customers to trade in their old devices remains a constraint on supply. The same applies to PCs and other equipment, said Jon Sansom, MD at GreenSafe IT. "Availability is a challenge," he said. Marcel Joosten, group director of marketing and digital commerce at tech lifecycle specialist XTENTEC, said the company now offers trade-ins when customers buy new kit. "We're actually financing the residual value" at the end of year two, three, or four, when customers return the equipment, he told the audience. XTENTEC collects, refurbishes, rents, and resells equipment, and has an agreement with HP to renovate aging products, with a two or even three-year warranty available as "just an SKU on the list from HP." Joosten said equivalent support, including HP Care Pack services, helped make refurbished equipment more attractive to buyers. Customers want to cut their carbon footprint, and many public and private sector tenders require it. But the "most important thing" for many is trust, said Patrick Molberg, CEO of Advania Finance. "The customers have to trust the refurbished equipment and have to trust the process. And I think one of the things that we have to be better at as a whole is that we kind of need to have a standard methodology regarding verification." Work on verification standards with vendors including HP, Lenovo, and Dell is ongoing, Molberg said. He also argued that lifecycle services should be built into purchasing decisions rather than added three or four years later. Joosten argued that listed US tech companies' focus on quarterly sales and market share can work against refurbishment. "That needs to change," he said. "I think there should be a market share figure for circularity." ®

item.title: Dev error bricked 600 PCs, caused $1M CD-ROM write-off
item.description: Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of " Who, Me? " – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software. This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal. Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time. In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption. "We wanted to increase our successful installation metrics, so in conjunction with the installation team, a key decision was made – by me – to force the updating of registry keys to enable the install," Oriel admitted. In his email to The Register , he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?" What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work. "Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote. The company decided the best thing to do was to tell affected customers they should go and buy a new PC – and that it would pick up the bill, no questions asked. "In the week prior to the holiday, we replaced over 600 machines," Oriel told The Register . Oriel and his developer colleagues were of course told to fix the problem but couldn't reproduce it nor figure out their mistake. "To get a reproduction case we need a user's machine where the user had created a Windows Registry restore point prior to installing our application," Oriel explained. If the developers could find such a machine, the plan was to roll it back to the restore point, verify everything was in order before the customer installed the update, install the accounting software, and figure out the problem. The company tasked its support agents with finding a customer willing to surrender their PC, which proved difficult because few bothered to create a registry restore point. item.description: The writer and podcaster on why politics is made to seem more complicated than it is and his mission to unpack world events for everyone Why did you get into comedy? My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else. Where do you find your material? item.title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
item.description: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post , the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April , developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI . Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

item.title: Huawei says it’s made a 100 percent Chinese PC
item.description: Huawei claims it’s built a desktop PC that uses only parts made in CHina. The company launched the Qingyun HM650 last week and said it uses Huawei’s own Kirin X90 processor, a ten-core 20-thread machine with a clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The machine runs a newly developed enterprise version of HarmonyOS, the OS Huawei developed to end its dependence on Android and which it intends to run on most of the devices it makes. A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That’s not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives. While Huawei has reportedly claimed local companies manufactured 100 percent of the components in the machine, it is unclear if all those components use Chinese designs. The Register mentions that uncertainty as many non-Chinese companies continue to operate factories in China. Even if Huawei is using some parts that aren’t entirely Chinese, the debut of the Qingyun HM650 is bad news for Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm, as all are suffering as the PC market shrinks due to the rising cost of memory. China’s government is an enormous buyer, and losing the chance to bid for its business is unlikely to be helpful. item.description: Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation into its CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair, amid allegations he had a romantic relationship with a woman US authorities feel is likely a Chinese spy. The AI hardware giant’s board published a statement on Sunday afternoon that says the company is “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The New York Times is the source of that reporting . On October 29 it alleged US government intelligence agencies decided to investigate a woman who goes by Alice Huang and/or Huang Le, on grounds she passes intelligence with Beijing. In that story The Times used the term “close relationship” to describe the Nvidia CEO's associations with both Ms Huang and US president Donald Trump. On Sunday the newspaper alleged US authorities believe Alice Huang and Jensen Huang shared a "romantic" relationship. The Times further alleges Ms Huang is a Chinese citizen who worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that has bought plenty of Nvidia hardware and is suspected of doing so to make it available to Chinese users, either by running inside datacenters or perhaps even facilitating transport to the Middle Kingdom. The US has for years banned or restricted exports of advanced GPUs to China, partly because it feels Beijing’s armed forces can use them to build systems that will erode America’s military superiority. Any relationship, of any sort, between Jensen Huang and a Chinese intelligence operative would therefore be enormously concerning. The company told the NYT that Jensen Huang and Alice Huang just had normal CEO-to-customer-exec chats that were no threat to Nvidia intellectual property or US national security. item.title: Doom delivers five minutes of terminal violence on an IBM mainframe
item.description: Can an IBM Z mainframe run Doom? Of course it can. The more interesting question is whether you can play it through a text terminal without ruining your eyesight. WND Software's browser demo connects to an IBM Z mainframe over SSH using its terminal emulator. Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII supplies the text-based carnage, replacing conventional graphics with colored characters. There's no sound. It is, however, completely playable (although you might need to recalibrate your vision to work out what is going on, particularly with regard to distant objects). Sessions are limited to five minutes, with room for up to 50 simultaneous users, but we had no trouble getting in. ASCII also presented no issues once the game was in motion. This writer played the original shareware release on an Amstrad ALT386SX portable, so squinting at an indistinct demon felt reassuringly familiar. That Doom can be persuaded to run on an IBM Z mainframe is not particularly noteworthy. The code has turned up everywhere from databases to PCB designers . Even the humble Pi Pico was roped into the fun. Keeping the action playable through a text terminal is the more entertaining achievement. A year ago, an IBM consultant persuaded Doom to run on IBM Z and LinuxONE using VNC to bring the pixelated mayhem to life. Using a terminal emulator, while a neat demonstration of the capabilities of WND's software, is perhaps more an example of "because I can" masochism. It's undeniably an enjoyable way to burn through five minutes. No installation or login required – just a willingness to shoot at punctuation. ®

item.title: Internet governance about to get its quadrennial stress test at ITU meeting
item.description: The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) kicks off its quadrennial plenipotentiary on Monday, and internet governance organizations are bracing in case the event becomes a forum for nation-states to try to challenge their roles. The ITU is the United Nations' specialized agency for information and communication technologies, meaning its members are nation-states. The body's role is to facilitate international connectivity, which it does by managing radio spectrum, satellite orbits, and working on relevant technical standards. Its key standards are pervasive. ITU-T X.509 sets out the rules of public key infrastructure. ITU-T E.164 governs telephone numbers. ITU-T H.264 and 265 define the video codecs used for most online streams. The ITU's role is largely uncontested, yet its work gets very close to that of the organizations who work on technologies that make the internet work. Those bodies include the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), which oversees the domain name system; and the regional internet registries (RIRs), which manage IP addresses. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) works on HTML, CSS, and accessibility. Governments participate in work at those internet governance bodies but are just one voice among many and can't override the consensus-driven decision-making process they use, under a system which has come to be known as the multi-stakeholder governance model. At a 2025 event called WSIS+20, the United Nations endorsed multi-stakeholder governance by deciding that its Internet Governance Forum (IGF) should become a permanent body. That decision effectively endorsed multi-stakeholder governance, and kept the ITU out of internet standards. Yet the IGF hasn't met since WSIS+20, so it is yet to start operating meaningfully as a permanent body. This year's ITU meeting is therefore a moment at which stakeholders can stress-test the delicate balance between the ITU, internet governance bodies, and the emerging IGF. Such a test could see ITU members try to have it pursue new fields that overlap with work performed by internet governance organizations. This has already happened before. China tried to have the ITU work on " New IP" – a major revision to internet protocol, a technology the IETF manages. In 2022, Russia and China backed a candidate for the ITU presidency who favored giving nations a stronger role in internet governance, potentially by having the ITU take over some standards work. That candidate was not elected. item.title: Fireworks says you’re wasting money on AI unless you’re using all the models
item.description: Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so. Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics." The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital. "You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said. For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said. "The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model." That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them. But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model. "We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this." The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library. "We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine. "And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. item.title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
item.description: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live." Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected. Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it. The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles. "It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report. The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026. According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online. item.title: Agents reveal secrets when offered to team up with each other
item.description: AI agents will break security rules, revealing their secrets to strangers, and running untrusted code in exchange for help from a swarm of other agents, according to test results shared with The Register . The test - part of an internal hackathon sponsored by the nonprofit AI Alignment Foundation and run by AE Studio - asked nine AI coding agents to fix a bug: a broken pricing service. The testers also gave the agents a private token, told them to keep it private, and gave them access to a forum of 24 other agents. The forum held the fix, and the swarm asked the nine to share their secret token and run an install script before they would help them fix the bug. Across 181 trials with that swarm, agents posted the token 15 percent of the time and ran the script 24 percent of the time, compared to 2 percent and 0 percent on an ordinary help forum. “It was like explicitly said that this is a secret key, and it should not be shared,” Diogo de Lucena, AE Studio's chief scientist, told The Register . “And in the first opportunity they saw,” the models shared the secret keys, “similar to some of the things that we've seen from OpenAI in the Hugging Face incident.” The Hugging Face incident - during which a swarm of OpenAI agents built unauthorized message boards to ask other agents for help, exploited zero-day vulnerabilities , gained internet access, stole credentials, and ultimately broke into Hugging Face - inspired this hackathon, de Lucena said. “Given the Hugging Face incident, and everything that's been happening since then, we thought that it made sense to start exploring behaviors that you might get from swarms, what risks are people not seeing yet,” he said. Sandboxed coding test This particular test from the hackathon that saw agents give up their keys to join a forum “is one of the most interesting ones,” according to de Lucena, who explained it has a huge impact on how organizations build IT systems and what access they grant to AI agents. “This was a fairly simple type of instructions - we were not particularly trying to get secretive information from the models,” he told us. “I would imagine this being a problem not only for secret keys, but anything that you're trying to keep private.” Plus, the agents' willingness to run an untrusted script on the host computer “seems like a pretty obvious risk,” he added. “You could get any kind of control over that host if you ran something malicious,” de Lucena said. “The simplicity of making that happen is very surprising. It's not surprising to me that you can get to it, but how little effort you need to put into setting that up to get models to share anything.” The researchers tested nine models: DeepSeek V4 Flash, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-5.6-Luna, and GPT-6.1-Sol, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5. item.title: PyTorch 2.15 tackles the 'one bad GPU' problem
item.description: ML admins will be happy to learn that one bad GPU may no longer mean starting an entire training job from scratch. The latest 2.15 release of PyTorch includes a rewritten backend for Nvidia's Collective Communications Library (NCCL), designed to improve fault diagnosis and recovery when GPUs work together. This latest feature shows how its creators continue to advance the software from being a tool for researchers to being a cornerstone in production AI work. The interface to the networking library in PyTorch needed a rewrite – it was drowning in technical debt, said PyTorch core developer Tristan Rice , a Meta software engineer specializing in distributed computing, during a live YouTube livestream on Thursday. NCCL is pronounced "Nickel" and stands for the Nvidia Collective Communications Library. It provides PyTorch with a set of inter-GPU communication primitives, allowing GPUs to communicate within a single-node or across multi-node clusters, which is vital for running inference on large neural networks and for other tasks in building and maintaining LLMs. The old NCCL interface was too chaotic The previous PyTorch backend for NCCL, called ProcessGroupNCCL , could spawn dozens of communicators per process group, leading to intermittent deadlocks and unpredictable performance. The new version of the NCCL backend comes with a strict rule: One process group gets only one communicator during initialization. By default, this rule eliminates crosstalk between multiple communicators and all the complexities that entails. If a program requires parallelism, it will have to dispatch more process groups. The updated library also better handles stragglers by allowing for easier reconfiguration. If a GPU crashes or runs slowly, a third-party orchestrator can exclude the laggard and even assign a replacement worker. A “flight recorder” has also been added to give admins a better idea of what went wrong. Previously, if a cluster of GPUs stalled—perhaps from a timeout or deadlock—the user would just get a generic message. The new flight recorder captures all operations in a series of snapshots that can be inspected after a failure occurs. Rice noted the cleaned-up NCCL backend, also called ProcessGroupNCCL, will give developers a blank slate, making it easier to add new features. The legacy ProcessGroupNCCL is part of the 2.15 package as a rollback, but if the new NCCL backend works as expected, the older version will be removed in the 2.16 release, planned for early next year. item.title: US air traffic control enters the 21st century, starts to abandon floppy disks
item.description: The Federal Aviation Administration still uses computers that require floppy disks. But those are finally on the way out within the next few years. Yes, it’s still 2026, and yes, you read that right: The FAA – the agency responsible for overseeing aviation safety in the US – is finally getting rid of four systems dating back to the 1980s that remain in use at more than 400 facilities around the country, the agency announced on Thursday. “Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in the FAA’s announcement. Only a few decades late, Sean, but we’re sure the flying public appreciates it. The new system, known as Enterprise Information Display System ( E-IDS ), is designed to consolidate data from various systems into a common digital platform, allowing air traffic controllers to access operational information and alerts needed to manage flights. E-IDS is replacing four legacy systems: Information Display System 4, used to track weather and operational info; the Automated Surface Observing System Controller Equipment Information Display System, which also relays weather information; the NAS Information Display System, which relays information about airports and other airspace conditions; and the En Route Information Display System (ERIDS), which handles information about flights. The FAA said E-IDS will improve how Pilot Reports and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. The agency has had its share of air traffic control SNAFUs, including one in 2023 that temporarily halted domestic flight departures nationwide after someone accidentally deleted a file from the NOTAM system. The FAA said it has already lined up five facilities to receive E-IDS upgrades: airports in Atlantic City, Nashville, and Rochester, New York, along with data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. The agency plans to install the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028. That 2028 deadline echoes the ambitious three-year timetable Duffy laid out last year for overhauling the nation's air traffic control system. Aside from the four systems E-IDS will replace, the FAA has a lot of outdated technology, with the Government Accountability Office saying in 2024 that 51 of the agency’s 138 ATC systems were unsustainable due to lack of parts and funding to sustain or replace them. Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA’s overhaul efforts, but that’s far short of what’s actually needed.
